extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in evolutionary biology and biostatistics (those measuring variation and studying evolution)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for quantifying types, variation, correlation, and selection in biological populations — how to measure 'type' and variability, represent distributions, distinguish normal vs abnormal variants, and test evolutionary factors quantitatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for quantitative demonstration of evolutionary factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Before accepting any cause as a factor of evolution one must not only show its plausibility but, if possible, demonstrate its quantitative validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not introduce new factors until the old have been tested; if new factors are suggested, show they are genuine causes of progressive change by giving a measure of their quantitative efficiency. The author admonishes biologists to attain the same certainty as physicists for their proposed factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify modes of change and their transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in living forms can arise from (i) modifications of individuals not due to growth/age (acquired modification) and (ii) modifications due to deaths/relative fertility (congenital), and these effects transmit either by inheritance or by tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing evolution, explicitly state which of the four processes (acquired modification via inheritance/tradition, congenital modification via inheritance/tradition) is invoked. Consider stability: tradition-based changes may be progressive but comparatively unstable and require selection to become permanent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection combined with heredity as the fundamental explanatory mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection (various kinds) combined with inheritance is the fundamental mode for describing changes in living forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize types of selection — autogeneric (within same type), heterogeneric (with allied/different types), inorganic (physical environment), and natural selection (all influences combined). Define 'naturally selected' as individuals better able to survive or leave more numerous/stronger progeny under given organic/inorganic environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish individual type from racial type; measure type by mode or mean
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuality (individual type) is given by modal or average values of characters within an individual; racial type is obtained by pooling across many individuals and taking the mode or mean for the race.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples (beech leaf vein counts, poppy stigmatic bands) to decide whether mode or mean is more appropriate; for small series mode may be unstable and average (mean) often preferable as 'type' measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure variation with distribution-sensitive metrics, not just range
rubrics_metrics.description: Range is a very rough estimate of variation because it gives no information about the distribution of frequencies within the range; good measures must be sensible to changes in frequency, especially of extreme variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer measures that reflect how frequently extremes occur rather than relying on min–max. The distribution of deviations and the relative numbers of extremes are crucial for evolutionary problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define deviation relative to the type (usually the mean)
rubrics_metrics.description: A deviation is the amount by which an individual differs in a given character from the type; deviations are considered negative or positive depending on being below or above the type value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deviations are usually measured from the mean. Use deviation counts (e.g. +3, −1.84) and tabulate their frequencies to assess how often particular deviations occur in a population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use frequency polygons and curves to represent distributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphically represent the distribution of deviations by plotting a frequency polygon (discrete) and, if desired, fit continuous frequency curves for concise description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale uniform lengths along the horizontal for character values and plot vertical frequencies; mathematicians should fit appropriate frequency curves to allow probability statements and to handle skew, bimodality, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard deviation as the preferred measure of variability (with computation rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard deviation (σ) — square root of the mean of squared deviations — provides a practical and theoretically useful measure of variability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute σ^2 by multiplying each type's frequency by the square of its deviation from the mean, summing these products and dividing by total N; take square root for σ. Other measures exist, but standard deviation recurs in many investigations and is usually best. Examples and numeric computations (poppy data) illustrate application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group continuous measurements into discrete units acknowledging measurement limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuous characters (e.g. bone lengths) must be grouped into discrete measurement units because absolute 'real' values are impractical due to measurement limits and biological variation with conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select sensible units (inches, mm, etc.) and group individuals falling within a unit together; proceed as with discrete quantities to find type and variability. Note slight corrections for continuous distributions when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish infrequent normal variation from abnormal variation and exclude accidental distortions
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual may show very infrequent but normal variation (still within continuous distribution) or a truly abnormal variation; avoid mislabeling infrequent normals as abnormal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider sample size: an apparently abnormal form (e.g. 18-band capsule) may be normal but very rare. Also exclude variations due to accidents of growth, injury, or pathological conditions. Museum practice may over-report infrequent normal variants as 'abnormal' if connecting links are not sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess fertility and frequency when judging evolutionary significance of abnormal variants
rubrics_metrics.description: For abnormal variations to contribute to evolution they must be sufficiently frequent and fertile; otherwise they will be swamped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistics on frequency and fertility of abnormal variations must be determined before asserting they are major drivers of evolution. Many abnormal variants are infertile (e.g. pathological giants/dwarfs) and thus unlikely to establish new races.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use selection experiments to test and shift population type
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificial selection — selecting individuals with extreme characters and resowing — can shift population type and demonstrate how selection operates to produce new races.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: de Vries obtained a buttercup with more petals via selection. Such experiments show how repeated selection of deviations can move the type beyond natural ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for sample size and probable errors before basing conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Small sample sizes produce unreliable estimates (e.g. standard deviations); probable errors must be considered before drawing valid arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns that for small series (individual poppies) one cannot place much stress on computed SDs; include error estimates and consider sampling variability in interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify correlation and regression among associated organs
rubrics_metrics.description: Correlation measures resemblance among associated organs (e.g. capsules on the same plant); regression describes how the associated value tends to 'regress' toward the population mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct correlation tables and compute means per column to observe regression phenomena: when one member has an extreme value the associated member tends to be nearer the population mean. Use large paired samples and present tabular and graphical summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare local races and environments to detect effects on type and variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect samples from different localities/environments to compare types and standard deviations and infer environmental or selection influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: poppies from different Chiltern sites and Quantocks show differences in mean and σ. Use such numerical differences for exact comparison and description of environmental/selection effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a probability framework to compute chances of character occurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the mathematical theory of chance to compute probabilities that a randomly selected individual will have certain character values (analogous to odds when casting a die).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From frequency polygons and fitted curves compute probabilities (e.g. percent with fewer than 9 bands). The duty of the mathematician is to find best frequency curves to describe distributions and allow such probability calculations.
